ops.insert: Vendor questionnaire: openEHR repository and Phoenix portal
Please answer each item in this same order for EHRbase, Better, Atomik, and vitagroup. Mark items included, optional, unavailable, or out of scope, and state assumptions and exclusions.
Identify the exact product, edition, release, and proposed service. Is this a CDR only, a managed EHRbase service, or a broader platform? List each included component.

Shared project brief: Phoenix Behavioral Health is evaluating an openEHR-guided clinical chart, clinical notes, and group notes in its existing portal. No clinical backend is selected or connected, and PHI should not be stored in Taskade.
The source product was referred to as “Kiboo”; its exact spelling, vendor, export options, and data volumes are not yet confirmed. Please separate discovery assumptions from confirmed facts.

Phoenix will fill in these shared quote assumptions once and send the same values to every vendor: sites [ ]; clinician/admin accounts by role [ ]; active patients [ ]; new patients/year [ ]; compositions/patient/year [ ]; attachments and storage [ ]; average/peak API volume [ ]; environments [ ]; region [ ]; availability target/support hours [ ]; retention period [ ]. Quote any alternative scale tiers using the same units.
State any information you need from Phoenix before giving a firm proposal. Do not substitute an unstated assumption for an unanswered item.
Which openEHR specifications, Reference Model, REST API versions, and conformance tests does the proposed release support? Provide links and any deviations.
Which AQL features and functions are supported in production? Identify unsupported or partial areas, limits, and query/versioning behavior.
Which additional APIs are included (for example FHIR, terminology, demographics, bulk import/export)? Give versions, conformance statements, rate limits, and licensing or usage fees.
How are templates, archetypes, terminology bindings, and local extensions authored, tested, promoted between environments, versioned, and retired?
How are composition versioning, correction/amendment, audit provenance, and retrieval of prior versions implemented and exposed through APIs?
Provide a working demonstration or documentation for storing and retrieving a behavioral-health clinical note and a group note, including patient/group association and access controls.
Which deployment models are available: vendor-hosted, customer cloud, on-premises, or hybrid? Specify who operates each layer and what the quote covers.
List supported cloud providers, regions, data-residency choices, network requirements, and environment topology. Are separate dev/test/staging/production environments priced separately?
Who handles provisioning, patching, upgrades, monitoring, capacity, certificates/secrets, incident response, and database administration? State customer responsibilities.
Provide availability commitment, measurement window, exclusions, service credits, maintenance windows, RTO, RPO, backup frequency, retention, and restore-test frequency.
Describe disaster recovery, incident communications, security patch timelines, release cadence, upgrade compatibility, and rollback procedures.
Which authentication standards and identity providers are supported (OIDC/OAuth2, SAML, other)? Explain issuer/audience validation, token lifetimes, key rotation, and service-account options.

Can the service enforce therapist-to-patient and admin permissions on every clinical API request, including reads, writes, search/AQL, exports, and background jobs? Describe policy model and enforcement point.
Can authorization use a delegated end-user identity or verified user claims, rather than one broadly privileged shared credential? Show how role and patient-care relationship changes take effect.

What audit events are available for viewing, querying, creating, amending, exporting, and administrative actions? Can logs be exported, retained, and correlated to an individual user and patient record?
Describe encryption in transit/at rest, key ownership and rotation, tenant isolation, vulnerability management, penetration testing, security attestations, and incident/breach notice terms.

Will you execute the required healthcare data-processing/BAA terms for the specific services and deployment quoted? Identify subprocessors, data locations, retention/deletion, and any service components excluded.
What source exports do you accept, and what source discovery is required? The current source was called “Kiboo”; please do not assume its vendor, format, or export capability.
Separate estimates and deliverables for discovery/profiling, extraction, mapping to openEHR templates, transformation, import, and production cutover. State what is excluded.
How will you preserve patient identifiers, source identifiers, authorship, encounter/group links, timestamps, attachments, amendments, and historical versions? Which elements cannot be carried over?
Describe mapping governance: who approves templates and mappings, how ambiguous or unmapped fields are handled, and how decisions are documented for later review.
What reconciliation reports, sample-based clinical validation, count/hash checks, error queues, and sign-off evidence are included? How are re-runs made safe and auditable?
State migration duration, Phoenix/vendor staffing, downtime or dual-running requirements, cutover/rollback plan, and assumptions by the shared volume tiers above.
Provide a phased implementation plan, milestones, acceptance criteria, Phoenix/vendor roles, required skills, and named deliverables. Separate template/API integration from historical migration.
Quote onboarding, architecture, template design, configuration, testing, training, go-live, and post-launch assistance separately, with estimated effort and dependencies.
What support hours, severity definitions, initial response and restoration targets, escalation path, named technical contact, and support languages are included at each tier?
For EHRbase-based offers, distinguish upstream community support from vendor-supported components and identify who owns incidents spanning custom code, infrastructure, and the CDR.
Provide customer references or production examples with comparable scale and clinical workflow, and identify any product roadmap dependency in your proposal.
Phoenix portal, Supabase, and Keragon integration
Recommend a supported portal-to-CDR pattern for the existing Phoenix portal. Identify what runs in the browser, the server-side API, the CDR, Supabase, and any workflow service.

Can the CDR trust our chosen identity issuer and authorize a signed-in therapist/admin for a specific patient on every request? Specify token exchange, claims, relationship lookup, revocation, and audit requirements.

If Supabase is used for portal operations but not the canonical clinical record, what integration pattern do you support? State whether you support Supabase Auth/JWT, Postgres, webhooks, or only custom APIs, and identify unsupported designs.

Can Keragon be used for asynchronous workflow events without becoming the clinical authorization boundary? Identify supported triggers/actions, identity context propagation, retries, idempotency, logging, and whether clinical data may pass through it under the proposed terms.
Provide a reference sequence or diagram for a portal read and write, including identity validation, therapist-to-patient authorization, audit, error handling, and any asynchronous integration.

Provide a line-item quote in USD for year 1, years 2-3, and a three-year total at the shared volume assumptions. Separate license/subscription, hosting, storage/usage, environments, implementation, migration, integration, support, and third-party charges.
List one-time and recurring charges, minimum terms, renewal/escalation rules, taxes, overages, usage meters, minimum commitments, and any fees not in the headline price.

Price the smallest evaluation environment and any trial separately. State duration, included services/support, production restrictions, conversion terms, and whether trial work is credited toward implementation.
What additional costs arise at each shared scale tier, including users, patients, compositions, queries, API calls, storage, environments, backups, and support?
Provide the price and process to export all clinical data, versions, audit records, templates, and attachments in documented, usable formats during the contract and at termination.
State contract term, termination assistance, data return/deletion timeline, deletion evidence, transition support, and any early termination or egress charges.
Attach the detailed quote, service description, SLA, architecture/data-flow diagram, security documents, API/conformance materials, and assumptions/exclusions. Confirm quote validity period.
2026-10-26 - openEHR comparison: hosting, support, APIs, migration, cost

EHRbase: Apache-2.0 open-source; can be self-deployed on-premises or in cloud, with Docker and PostgreSQL 15+ in its current quick-start/deployment notes. Offers openEHR REST and AQL. OAuth2 support exists, but therapist-to-patient relationship authorization still needs application policy. No license fee, but production infrastructure, engineering, backups, monitoring, upgrades, and support determine total cost. Sources: https://github.com/ehrbase/ehrbase and https://docs.ehrbase.org/docs/EHRbase/Explore/openEHR-REST

Better Platform: public product material says it can be hosted by Better, run in the customer cloud, or on-premises, delivered by Better, its delivery partners, or the customer team. Its integrated clinical repository is openEHR and its operational repository is FHIR, with an API layer and app-building tools. Commercial terms/pricing and support SLA were not published in the reviewed pages; request a scoped quote. It may reduce platform assembly, but does not remove source-data extraction and mapping work. Sources: https://www.better.care/better-platform/ and https://www.better.care/request-a-demo/

CaboLabs Atomik: offers self-hosted deployments and managed deployment. For self-hosting, the vendor says the commercial license includes updates/documentation, with support packages separate; managed deployment includes infrastructure, updates, monitoring, and initial configuration. Public docs say openEHR ITS REST, a working subset of AQL, and a custom FHIR R4/R5 facade. CaboLabs estimates template/API integration may take days to weeks for many projects; that is not a legacy-data migration or production-rollout estimate. Pricing is quote-based by deployment, scale, and support. Sources: https://cabolabs.com/our_software/atomik/faq, https://cabolabs.com/our_software/atomik/documentation, and https://cabolabs.com/our_software/atomik/pricing

vitagroup HIP EHRbase / HIP: vendor materials describe AWS Marketplace deployment options. The HIP listing offers a three-month test-and-learn period, custom pricing, and technical support under trial SLAs. EHRbase brings its openEHR REST/AQL interface; for the fuller HIP offer, confirm which APIs, managed operations, SLAs, and support are included in the proposed package. Source: https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-67vuu6cts7p2c and https://hip.vitagroup.ag/en/vitagroup-aws-innovation/

Migration effort cannot be responsibly estimated yet: the source product name is still unconfirmed (user said “Kiboo”), and exports, data volumes, note formats, identifiers, attachments, and historical data requirements are unknown. All options require source extraction, field/concept mapping to openEHR templates, validation, reconciliation, and cutover testing. Template/API implementation and historical-data conversion are distinct estimates. No Taskade patient submissions were migrated.

Comparable quote checklist: separate license/subscription, hosting, environment count, storage and usage, implementation/templates, migration, integrations, support/SLA, backup/restore, upgrades, and exit/data export. Ask each vendor to price the same patient/composition volumes, environments, availability target, and support window. Public reviewed materials did not provide directly comparable production total-cost figures.
2026-10-26 - openEHR repository options and portal fit

EHRbase: active open-source openEHR CDR; project describes RM 1.1.0, openEHR REST API, model-based validation, and AQL queries. Best for a team wanting control and willing to own deployment, upgrades, monitoring, backups, and support. Sources: https://github.com/ehrbase/ehrbase and https://docs.ehrbase.org/docs/EHRbase/Explore/openEHR-REST

Better Platform: commercial broader platform combining an openEHR clinical repository, FHIR operational repository, integration hub, and Better Studio low-code tooling. Potentially less assembly across the CDR and app-building layers; confirm product scope, deployment/hosting, contract, support, and total cost directly. Source: https://www.better.care/better-platform/

CaboLabs Atomik: vendor-described openEHR clinical and demographic repository with template-defined structure and persistent API-backed storage. A commercial option to evaluate if the goal is a repository without assembling the whole platform. Verify deployment model, support, pricing, and available interfaces with the vendor. Sources: https://cabolabs.com/our_software/atomik and https://cabolabs.com/our_software/atomik/features

vitagroup HIP EHRbase / HIP CDR: vendor-supported EHRbase and a wider health-data platform are listed by vitagroup. Worth comparing when operational support is important; confirm whether the offered deployment is a CDR-only service or the fuller HIP platform. Source: https://www.vitagroup.ag/en/products/

Architecture fit: keep the selected openEHR CDR as the canonical store for clinical compositions, versions, and clinical queries. Use Supabase for the portal's relational/operational records only if that split suits Phoenix; do not assume an openEHR CDR can safely use Supabase as its internal database. Put the browser behind a server-side API that verifies the signed-in identity and therapist/admin-to-patient relationship before each clinical read/write.

Keragon: its public PostgreSQL integration and HTTP webhook trigger support make it plausible for asynchronous integrations and event-driven tasks. The reviewed public material did not establish per-request forwarding of the portal user's identity or enforcement of Supabase RLS, so treat it as workflow plumbing, not the clinical authorization boundary. Source: https://www.keragon.com/integrations/postgresql and https://help.keragon.com/hc/en-us/articles/26592306434578-Using-the-HTTP-Webhook-Trigger

Supabase RLS can enforce policies from verified JWT claims; Supabase warns its service-role secret bypasses RLS and must stay server-side. Taskade OIDC-to-Supabase token trust has not been established, so validate issuer/audience/signature and user/therapist mapping before selecting the auth path. The current portal's patient-submission projects remain on Taskade and were not migrated by the shell work. Sources: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security, https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/third-party/overview, and portal guide: https://www.taskade.com/d/BfcUk3WBCosXNt9d
